lead: An AM transmitter makes a stable carrier, impresses the audio on its amplitude and delivers kilowatts to the antenna. Where the audio enters decides the design. In a low-level transmitter the carrier is modulated at a few watts and the AM wave is then raised to full power by linear amplifiers, which keep the envelope but waste power. In a high-level transmitter the carrier is amplified unmodulated by efficient class C stages, and the audio varies the supply of the final stage, so the modulator must itself be a large audio amplifier. Large medium-wave broadcast stations use high-level modulation; small and wideband transmitters use low-level.
prereq: You need: the power formula Pt = Pc(1 + m²/2) from AM: modulation index, spectrum and power and the modulators of AM generation: square-law and balanced modulators.

blocks.text: Both designs start the same way. A crystal oscillator sets the carrier frequency to within a few parts per million. A buffer amplifier follows it, so that later stages, whose load changes with tuning and modulation, cannot pull the oscillator off frequency. Where the crystal is cut for a lower frequency, class C frequency multipliers (doublers or triplers) bring the carrier to f<sub>c</sub>. A class C amplifier conducts for less than half a cycle and delivers current pulses into a tuned tank, which rings at the carrier frequency. It reaches 70 % to 80 % efficiency because its transistor or valve is either off or fully on, but its output amplitude is not proportional to its input. That last fact shapes everything that follows.

Low-level. The carrier is modulated in an early stage at small power, for example with a balanced or base modulator, and the AM wave is then amplified to full power. Every stage after the modulator must be linear, or the envelope distorts and splatters into neighbouring channels. These linear amplifiers are class A, B or AB; a practical design uses class AB push-pull with negative feedback, since pure class B has crossover distortion. Their efficiency is lower than class C. The audio stage is small, since it only drives a low-power modulator.

High-level. The carrier is amplified unmodulated through class C driver stages, and the audio is applied to the final stage. In collector (or anode) modulation, the audio power amplifier, usually class B push-pull, is connected through a modulation transformer in series with the DC supply of the final class C stage. The supply then becomes VCC[1 + m cos 2πfmt]. A class C stage with a tuned tank gives an RF output amplitude proportional to its supply voltage, so the output is AM.

The sidebands get their power from the modulator. If the class C stage takes P<sub>dc</sub> from the supply with efficiency η, the carrier is P<sub>c</sub> = ηP<sub>dc</sub>. Varying the supply by the factor [1 + m cos 2πf<sub>m</sub>t] raises its average input power to P<sub>dc</sub>(1 + m²/2), so the modulator must supply
P<sub>audio</sub> is the audio power in watts the modulator delivers to the final stage; η is the final stage's efficiency. At m = 1 this is half the DC input, a very large audio amplifier.

blocks.text: The deciding point is linearity against efficiency. A low-level chain must keep every later stage linear and pays for it in heat. A high-level chain keeps its RF stages efficient but needs the modulation transformer and an audio amplifier rated at about half the carrier power. SSB and VSB transmitters have no carrier to modulate in the final stage, so they are always low-level.

examples.question: A high-level transmitter delivers a 10 kW carrier from a class C final of efficiency 75 %, collector-modulated to m = 0.8 by a class B modulator of efficiency 65 %. Find the DC input of the final, the audio power the modulator supplies, the sideband and total output powers, the power drawn by the modulator and the overall efficiency.
steps: Sidebands: P<sub>c</sub> m²/2 = 10 × 0.32 = 3.2 kW, which is η × P<sub>audio</sub> = 0.75 × 4.27 kW. Total P<sub>t</sub> = 10 × 1.32 = 13.2 kW.
Check: the final takes 13.33 + 4.27 = 17.6 kW and gives 13.2 kW, still 75 %.
The modulator draws 4.27/0.65 = 6.56 kW from its own supply.
examples.answer: P<sub>dc</sub> = 13.33 kW, P<sub>audio</sub> = 4.27 kW, sidebands 3.2 kW, P<sub>t</sub> = 13.2 kW; modulator input 6.56 kW; overall efficiency 66.3 %.

examples.question: A low-level transmitter modulates a 2 W carrier to m = 0.8 and amplifies it with a 20 dB linear amplifier of average efficiency 50 %. Find the output carrier, sideband and total powers and the amplifier's DC input.
steps: 20 dB is a power ratio of 10<sup>20/10</sup> = 100.
Carrier: 2 × 100 = 200 W. Sidebands: 200 × 0.64/2 = 64 W. Total 264 W.
DC input: 264/0.50 = 528 W, of which 264 W becomes heat in the amplifier.
examples.answer: 200 W carrier, 64 W sidebands, 264 W total; the amplifier draws 528 W.

traps: Putting a class C amplifier after a low-level modulator. Its output is not proportional to its input, so it flattens the envelope.
Thinking the sideband power in high-level AM comes from the RF chain. It comes from the audio modulator through the supply.
Sizing the modulator as P<sub>c</sub> m²/2. It must deliver P<sub>dc</sub> m²/2 = P<sub>c</sub> m²/(2η): 4.27 kW, not 3.2 kW, in the example.
Taking 20 dB as ×20. For power it is ×100.

quiz.q: List the stages of a high-level AM transmitter in order.
quiz.a: Crystal oscillator, buffer, frequency multipliers and class C drivers, class C final with a collector modulator fed by an audio amplifier, then the antenna matching network.

quiz.q: Why is a buffer placed after the crystal oscillator?
quiz.a: It isolates the oscillator from later stages whose load changes, so the carrier frequency does not shift.

quiz.q: A 5 kW carrier is modulated to m = 0.6. Find the total power and the sideband power.
A collector-modulated final takes 20 kW DC. Find the audio power needed for m = 1.
How does collector modulation turn a class C amplifier into an AM modulator?
quiz.a: The output amplitude of a class C stage with a tuned tank is proportional to its supply. The audio varies the supply as V<sub>CC</sub>[1 + m cos 2πf<sub>m</sub>t], so the RF amplitude follows the audio.

quiz.q: Why are SSB transmitters always low-level?
quiz.a: SSB has no carrier and its envelope swings to zero. It must be generated at low power and carried by linear amplifiers; a supply-modulated class C final needs a steady carrier to vary.

quiz.q: Compare the efficiency of the two worked examples and explain the difference.
quiz.a: The high-level set turns 66.3 % of its total input into RF, the low-level set's amplifier 50 %. The high-level RF stages are class C and the audio is handled by one modulator; the low-level linear stages waste power on every RF cycle.

beyond: Most medium-wave transmitters built in recent decades are solid state and modulate the supply digitally: pulse-step modulation switches many small DC modules in and out to build the envelope at high efficiency. Envelope tracking in mobile phone amplifiers applies the same idea to linear transmitters. Search next for pulse-step modulation and envelope tracking.

figure.caption: The two worked examples. Low-level: a 2 W carrier is modulated, then a 20 dB linear amplifier gives 264 W from 528 W of DC. High-level: class C stages amplify the bare carrier and the audio modulator varies the final stage supply, giving 13.2 kW at m = 0.8.
